name: Wirangu-Nauo
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern
earlier_scan.source_named: Hercus, Luise A. 1999. A Grammar of the Wirangu Language from the West Coast of South Australia. Pacific Linguistics C-150 (sec on accent and pitch); PDF read at sealang.net/archives/pl/pdf/
earlier_scan.note: Fixed initial stress; secondary stress on third syllable in 4+ syllable words; shifts to final syllable in emphatic vocatives/imperatives.

new_statements.quote: The regular accent in Wirangu is on the first syllable of a word, as is the case in all the surrounding languages. It is a fairly heavy stress accent (here marked by ˌ preceding the stressed syllable). The accent is accompanied by a high pitch intonation. There is a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables (this is here marked by ˮ preceding the syllable that bears the secondary accent). There are however a few situations in which this can vary. In emphatic vocatives and imperatives the accent can shift to the final syllable, which can then show vowel distortion

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (240 pp., text present; sealang.net CC BY-SA 2015 edition of Pacific Linguistics C-150, DOI 10.15144/PL-C150). The stated locator is right: printed p. 35 = PDF page 57, section 2.2.2 'Accent and vowel length', (a) 'Accent and pitch'. There is a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables (this is here marked by " preceding the syllable that bears the secondary accent). There are…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word; a secondary stress on the third syllable in words of four or more syllables (pattern 1, 10, 100, 1010, 10100..). The primary accent carries high pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables (p. 35). Disyllabic case suffixes -ngorni (ablative) and -birna (elative) 'bear at least a secondary stress' (p. 46); the postinflectional apprehensional clitic -dhirdi 'normally has at least some minor accent on the first syllable' (p. 129).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) In emphatic vocatives and imperatives the accent can shift to the final syllable, which then shows vowel distortion, e.g. ['wiya] 'mother' vs [ˮwi'yai] 'eh, mother!', ['urldiga] 'come here!' vs [ˮurldi'gei] (pp. 35, 62, 117-118); bare-stem urgent imperatives show no shift, only a stronger initial accent with raised pitch (p. 118). (2) With the suffix -gardu/-garda after an a-final stem, the main stress optionally falls on the long aa created by elision of the suffix's g (marnaardu [ˮma'rnaardu] 'very big'), the initial syllable then having secondary accent; optionally the main accent stays initial with high pitch for extreme emphasis (p. 35-36).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('on the first syllable of a word'), based on the author's fieldwork with the last speakers (1960s-1990s); the vocative/imperative shifts are emphatic, phrase-final utterance phenomena. Vowel length is non-phonemic (all monosyllables long), so no weight interaction is described.
new_statements.identity_note: wira1260 'Wirangu-Nauo' [wiw] is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping entry, split in 2012 (ISO 639-3 CR 2011-133) into Wirangu wira1265 [wgu] and Nauo nauo1235 [nwo] after Hercus & Simpson (2001, 2004) showed Nauo to be a separate language. The quoted statement describes Wirangu (wira1265) only, as spoken on the west coast of South Australia (Hercus's speakers from the Ceduna/Koonibba area). Nauo is known from ~13 secure 19th-century words (Hercus & Simpson 2001) and has no stress description; the catalog entry should be filed under wira1265.

sources.citation: Hercus, Luise & Jane Simpson. 2001. The tragedy of Nauo. In J. Simpson, D. Nash, M. Laughren, P. Austin & B. Alpher (eds), Forty years on: Ken Hale and Australian languages, 263-290. Pacific Linguistics 512. DOI 10.15144/PL-512.263.
sources.note: No statement on Nauo stress. Only fn. 16 (p. 272) notes that Provis (1879) used an acute accent to mark stress in his wordlist; Table 5 (p. 283) covers phonotactics (C-final words, prestopping etc.), not accent. Establishes Nauo as a separate language from Wirangu, known from ~13 secure words.
